Act three. Enough background. Now we watch a platform decide, live, on a system small enough to run on this laptop.

Source: Ch 14.

KASPER

This is the book's blueprint for a governed agent platform, cropped to what the demo touches. The numbers are the five building blocks the abstract promised: 1, the agent runtime. 2, the context layer. 3, the tool gateway. 4, the policy and eval pipeline, which is two boxes: 4a policy, 4b evals. 5, multi-agent over shared context, underneath. The unnumbered boxes, tools, models and telemetry, are what the blocks stand on.

Read it like this. On the left, the path a request takes: runtime, gateway, then tools and models. Under it, policy, which the gateway asks on every call that matters. On the right, the path the evidence takes: telemetry, then evals. Each chip says how much Northstar shows. Gateway, policy and evals: shown, in depth. Runtime and telemetry: partial. Two blocks are missing: 2, the context layer, meaning memory and retrieval, and 5, multi-agent over shared context. Better you hear that now than in Q&A.

Source: Ch 11 (Figure 11.1, section 11.2).

KASPER

William said none of this is new. Here's what he meant. Read each row left to right. On the left, something your platform team already runs. On the right, the same idea pointed at agents. A golden path becomes a declared contract per agent. Admission policy becomes a decision at the tool gateway. Service identity becomes one SPIFFE identity per agent. Your observability stack learns GenAI traces and decision spans. A feature flag becomes the autonomy level, changed live. And the catalog becomes the view onto all of it. The last column is where each one lives in Northstar. So don't start an AI platform from scratch. Teach the one you have about agents.

Source: Ch 1 (Figure 1.8), Ch 11.

KASPER

So what makes a foundation governed, not just connected? Northstar comes up in six stages, and each adds one thing you can prove. Read the stair left to right. One, connected: the agents talk, and one trace covers the claim. That's plumbing. Two is the line: the platform starts deciding, and identity is an input to that decision. Three: a human can overturn a refusal. Four: prove why money moved, from telemetry alone. Five: one live value changes what's allowed, no redeploy. Six: Backstage is just the view. The grey line under each is what that stage installs. Today we run stage six.

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §1 and §3 (Option 1); Ch 4, Ch 11.

KASPER

Here is Northstar. A customer files claim CLM-1842. The claims agent checks it with plain rules, no model, and hands it on. The settlement agent is the only one with a model, Claude. To pay, it calls agentgateway, not the payment tool. The gateway checks who is calling, then asks the policy service, hop 3p, whether this payment is allowed. Only on a yes does it forward to payments-mcp and the ledger. Model calls go straight to Anthropic, not through the gateway. Cilium makes the gateway the only road to the tool. Everything reports to one Collector, at one hundred percent. Next: the rule behind this picture, then each tool.

[verify: pinned versions (agentgateway v1.5.0, Cilium 1.20.1, a2a-sdk 0.3.7) before November, Appendix B]

Source: Ch 4 (Figure 4.5).

KASPER

The design rule as a picture. Left: the model can request anything, even six thousand two hundred euros. Middle: one choke point the agent can't skip. Who is asking, and is it allowed? Right: only a permit becomes an effect. Why not limit the agent? An agent that can choose to ask permission can choose not to. The tool? That's an if-statement with extra steps. A test fails if one ever appears. And that middle box hides two different jobs. Next slide.

Source: Ch 4 (Figure 4.4, design principle 2), Ch 7 (Decision 2).

KASPER

Two words you'll hear from here on. An enforcement point stands at the door. Think of a bouncer. It lets a call through or stops it, and that's all it does. A decision point knows the rules. Think of the manager. The bouncer asks, the manager answers, and the manager never touches the door. In Northstar the bouncer is agentgateway, and the manager is our policy decision service. Keep them apart, and you can change the rule without touching the door.

Source: Ch 7; docs/architecture.md "The decision the platform makes".

KASPER

Every tool, grouped by the job it does. Read the top row first: the claim path. A2A is how agents talk to each other; MCP is how an agent calls a tool. Both now sit in the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation. Cilium, the network, makes the gateway the only road to the tool. SPIFFE and SPIRE give each agent pod a signed identity. agentgateway checks it and asks for a decision. The Policy Decision Service is our own code: permit or deny, and why. OpenFeature and flagd hold the autonomy level. Bottom row, around the path: the Collector takes every span, unsampled, to Jaeger, OpenSearch and Prometheus. Our eval-scorer writes scores back into the trace. Backstage is the view. The tinted chips mark code we wrote.

KASPER

Workload identity. A name tag says who you claim to be. A passport is issued by someone else, checked at the border, and valid for one destination. SPIFFE is the standard for the name. SPIRE is the passport office. Follow the numbers. One: a ClusterSPIFFEID says which pods get which ID, and the controller-manager turns it into a registration. Two: the CSI driver mounts SPIRE's Workload API socket into the settlement-agent pod. Three: when the agent asks, the SPIRE agent checks the pod's namespace and ServiceAccount. Four: SPIRE issues a JWT-SVID for one audience, the gateway. Five: the gateway checks the signature against keys the OIDC discovery provider publishes, and writes jwt.sub on its span. Trust domain: northstar.local. One thing SPIRE does not do is emit spans. Metrics only.

[verify: SPIRE 1.15.3 still has no OTLP or tracing support]

Source: deploy/platform/spire/registration.yaml and values.yaml; agents/settlement-agent/svid.py; docs/architecture.md "Workload identity"; Ch 7.

KASPER

Before the config, what kind of thing is agentgateway?

Look left first. An ordinary API gateway sees an HTTP request: a POST to slash mcp, a host, a token. The body is just bytes to it. So it can make rules about URLs.

Now the right. agentgateway speaks the agent protocols. It opens the message and sees a tools/call, for the tool execute_payment, for six thousand two hundred euros, from settlement-agent. So it can make rules about the tool call itself. Think of a post office that only reads the envelope, next to a customs officer who opens the parcel.

Along the bottom: one proxy for three kinds of traffic. MCP, agent to tool. A2A, agent to agent. And LLM, agent to model. In our demo it guards one road: the MCP road to the payments tool. And Cilium makes sure it's the only road.

[verify: agentgateway v1.5.0 feature set: MCP, A2A and LLM routes; still LF/AAIF]

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml (one mcp backend, payments-mcp); tools/payments-mcp/server.py; docs/architecture.md "Hop 3".

KASPER

Now its config. agentgateway is written in Rust, and it's a Linux Foundation project, in the Agentic AI Foundation, not CNCF. Our whole setup is one YAML file. Read it left to right: every tool call passes three checks, in this order. One, jwtAuth: who is asking? A bad or missing token gets HTTP 401 before the gateway even reads the MCP message. Two, mcpGuardrails: is it allowed? The gateway sends the call over gRPC to the policy service, and waits. failClosed means: if the policy service can't answer, the answer is no. A deny stops right here. Three: on a permit, the gateway drops the token and forwards. The tool never sees the agent's credential. Underneath, every step writes a span. You'll see them in a minute.

[verify: agentgateway v1.5.0 still the latest stable before November; check the v1.6 pre-releases]

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml; docs/architecture.md "Hop 3"; Ch 6, Ch 7.

KASPER

The live policy uses OpenFeature, so here's what that is.

OpenFeature is a CNCF standard for asking about feature flags. The question is standard. What answers it is pluggable. Think of a wall socket: every appliance fits the same socket, whatever power station is behind it.

Read the stack from the top. Our policy service asks one question: what is the autonomy level, for this SPIFFE ID? The OpenFeature SDK is the same API in every language, and it has hooks. We use the OpenTelemetry hook. Under it, a provider plugs in a backend. Ours is flagd, over gRPC on localhost. And the flag itself lives in a FeatureFlag, a Kubernetes object. The OpenFeature Operator puts the flagd sidecar in the pod for us.

Now the right: why use a flag for a policy knob? It changes without a deploy. The change is a one-word diff you can review. It's answered per caller. And every evaluation leaves evidence.

[verify: OpenFeature still CNCF Incubating; Open Feature Operator v0.9.3, flagd v0.16.2, openfeature-sdk 0.10.0 (Python)]

Source: platform/policy-decision-service/pds/autonomy.py and requirements.txt; deploy/platform/openfeature/featureflag.yaml and featureflagsource.yaml; deploy/k8s/policy-decision-service.yaml (openfeature.dev annotations).

KASPER

And this is the manager, the policy decision service, our own code. Read the right side first: the rule table. It has two keys: who is calling, and the autonomy level. settlement-agent at assisted may execute up to six thousand euros. At autonomous, a million. No row means deny. Now the left: where the level comes from. The FeatureFlag you just met, read through the flagd sidecar. If flagd can't answer, the level falls back to assisted. Every answer becomes a policy.decision span. The other key, identity, comes back after the demo.

Source: platform/policy-decision-service/pds/rules.py and pds/autonomy.py; deploy/platform/openfeature/featureflag.yaml; docs/architecture.md (flagd row); Ch 7, Ch 8.

KASPER

SAY: Here's what you're about to see. A customer files a vehicle-damage claim. Agents settle it. The platform decides. We run one claim, CLM-1842, twice. Claim A asks for six thousand two hundred euros, just over the junior agent's six-thousand limit: refused. Claim B asks for five thousand eight hundred: executed, no human anywhere. You need both. A platform that refused everything would look the same on the first run. Then the same six thousand two hundred succeeds three ways. A human approves it. The contract is flipped with kubectl. And the same flip in Backstage, which is the point: Backstage is only the view. Today you'll see the human and the Backstage flip live. These are the five screens I'll switch between.

PRE-FLIGHT: confirm before you start (runbook §4, T-10 and T-5)
1. setup-kind.sh printed ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: SET. start-demo.sh is running in its own terminal, and its output has a Backstage line, not "Backstage: SKIPPED".
2. Every pod Running: kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | grep -v ' Running \| Completed ' || echo "all Running" prints "all Running".
3. The contract is resting and refusing: kubectl -n northstar-platform get featureflag northstar-autonomy -o jsonpath='{.spec.flagSpec.flags.autonomy-level.state}{"  default="}{.spec.flagSpec.flags.autonomy-level.defaultVariant}{"\n"}' prints "ENABLED  default=assisted", and the targeting jsonpath shows both branches "assisted".
4. Backstage, localhost:7007, Guest then Enter works; the Autonomy contract card (localhost:7007/autonomy-contract) reads assisted for settlement-agent and for senior-settlement-agent.
5. Tabs open and loaded: 8080, 8081, 16686 (service dropdown populated), 5601, 7007.
6. At T-5 the rehearsal claim of 6200 came back refused, and the ledger was reset after it: kubectl -n northstar-systems rollout restart deploy/payments-api.

ORDER OF BEATS in this talk: Beat 1 live (8080), Beat 2 live (16686), Beat 3 as a slide, Beat 4 live (8081, then Jaeger), Beat 7 live (7007, then 8080, then Jaeger), then Beats 5 and 6 as slides in Act 4. Beat 7 flips the contract to autonomous: it must be flipped back to assisted before leaving that beat.

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §1, §2, §4, §6.

KASPER

Beat 1 · live · customer UI.

1. DO: switch to the customer UI tab, http://localhost:8080. The form is pre-filled: claim CLM-1842, policy POL-77120, amount 6200. Change nothing.
2. DO: click Submit claim. It's a real model call; keep talking for the few seconds it takes.
3. SHOW: the Outcome block. Expected shape: status "refused", a paymentId PAY-0000NN, amount 6200, and a narrative in the model's own words, different every run.
4. SAY, at once, before anyone reads it as a bug: "That is not a failure. That is the platform working. The agent proposed the payment. The platform refused to execute it. And notice the narrative is different every time you run this, because it is genuinely the model explaining its own refusal, not a canned string."
5. DO: change the amount to 5800. Click Submit claim again.
6. SHOW: status "executed".
7. SAY: "Same claim, same agents, same path, four hundred euros apart. One is refused and one goes through. A platform that refused everything would have looked identical on the first run alone. That is why you always see both."
8. Back on the slide: point at the line at six thousand and the rule name under it.

HAZARDS
- Don't let "refused" land as an error. Name it the success first.
- Never promise or read out a payment id. They count up from the ledger pod's last restart.
- Don't close or reload the tab right after a submit: the browser sends its spans in batches every five seconds.
- First claim errors: most likely the API key. Go to the fallback slide.
- 6200 comes back executed: the contract was left autonomous. Say so, flip it back to assisted, resubmit.

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §5 beat 1, §7, §8; Ch 4 (Figure 4.1), Ch 14.

Beat 2 · live · Jaeger. Open with: each line in a trace is a span, one timed step, indented under the step that called it.

1. DO: Jaeger tab, http://localhost:16686. Service customer-ui, Operation claim.submit, click Find Traces.
2. Ignore any harness-probe services in the dropdown: those are the test suite's own spans. If a count reads 0 while traces are listed, that's Jaeger's "total" quirk. Trust the list.
3. DO: open the six-thousand-two-hundred trace: the one with errors, second from the top after beat 1. If it opens in the GenAI view, switch the view menu top right to Trace Timeline. The Find box jumps to a span by name.
4. SHOW four spans, opening each:
 a. claim.submit, customer-ui: the root. No parent. Point at northstar.claim.id=CLM-1842.
 b. tools/call, agentgateway, under execute_tool execute_payment: point at jwt.sub, the caller's attested SPIFFE ID, set by the gateway from the token it checked.
 c. policy.decision: point at deny, the rule settlement-agent.assisted.execute_limit, 6200 requested, 6000 allowed.
 d. Guardrail: point at grpc.status 0.
5. SAY: "Look at the status on policy.decision. It is not ERROR. A refusal is the platform working. If it were an error, every dashboard you own would page you for correct behaviour."
6. SAY: "And Guardrail says gRPC status zero. That's how 'the policy said no' stays different from 'the policy service was down'."
7. SHOW the absence: no payments-mcp execute_payment span, no payments-api execute span. On the slide, the struck-through lines.
8. SAY: "The execute call never reached the tool. The absence of those spans is the evidence that nothing happened, rather than something happening and failing." That holds only because we never sample.

KASPER

Now we read what the bouncer writes down, for one permitted payment. Follow the numbers. One: tools/call, the request as it arrived. Twenty-two keys. jwt.sub is who asked, and gen_ai.tool.name is the only place the tool is named. Two: Guardrail, nine keys: the gateway phoning the policy service. grpc.status zero means the call worked, not what the answer was. Three: the policy service's span holds the why: rule, limit, amount. Four: the outbound call, six keys, and no jwt.sub, because the token was stripped. At the bottom: the four keys a refusal adds to span one. On a deny, span four doesn't exist.

[verify: check for agentgateway v1.6.0 GA and re-run test_gateway_trace.py before November; the key sets may change, Appendix B]

Source: Ch 6 (Figures 6.7, 6.9 to 6.12, 6.15).

KASPER

Read the big number first. Two hundred is the HTTP status of the refused payment. The gateway marks its span ERROR with reason MCP, but the refusal travels as an error message inside a successful HTTP response. A sealed envelope delivered on time, with a no inside. "Anyone alerting on HTTP status alone will not see this refusal at all." Metrics don't help. No agentgateway metric counts permit versus deny, and the Guardrail histogram counts every check, whatever the answer. In Northstar none of it reaches Prometheus anyway: nothing scrapes the gateway's port. The small line: v1.5.0 still writes the old attribute name. So alert on the decision span.

[verify: v1.6.0 GA status and PR #3182; whether a permit/deny metric has been added, Appendix B]
